title: Rabbit-Proof Fence
full_review:
A trio of aboriginal girls legally torn from their mothers in 1931 begins the punishing 1,200-mile walk home in the wrenching, fact-based drama, "Rabbit-Proof Fence" (Miramax).

Australian director Philip Noyce deserts his usual Hollywood action fare to tell the story of the Australian government's campaign to eliminate "half castes" -- Aborigines of mixed blood.

Spurning sentimentality, he delivers a riveting story of perseverance and courage that is almost unbelievable were it not based on the book by one of the surviving girl's daughters, Doris Pilkington Garimara. Government policy allowed police to forcibly remove children of mixed race from the Outback to distant camps where they were made to abandon their culture and language in preparation to become domestics and farm workers in white homes.

A.O. Neville (Kenneth Branagh), the bureaucrat in charge of Aborigines, authorizes the removal of sisters Molly (Everlyn Sampi), 14, and Gracie (Laura Monaghan), 8, and their 10-year-old cousin, Daisy (Tianna Sansbury). Ripped from their sobbing, grasping mothers, the girls are spirited away, put in a train cage and on a truck until their arrival at the forbidding Moore River Native Settlement.

In short order, Molly decides they must escape and head home despite the distance -- and the certainty of isolation and beatings if they are recaptured.

Their arduous journey begins and a native tracker (David Gulpilil) is sent on their trail, requiring Molly to be especially resourceful in not leaving footprints in the sand and mud. Random encounters with strangers along the way provide them with food and water as they use the country's rabbit-proof fence that keeps rabbits off the farmland as their directional guide to get home.

Meanwhile, Neville adds cops to the pursuit, fearing the bad publicity that might result, but the native tracker begins to respect the girls' dogged determination as the weeks wear on. At a crossroads, Daisy decides to take a different path from the sisters, but Molly and little Gracie soldier on, unwilling to give up even as starvation and delirium threaten their very lives.

The barren, harshly lit landscapes and eerie nightscapes place the viewer in the frightening situation the children endured for nine long weeks. Nor could Noyce have found a better cast than these three girls who never acted before; their solemn faces and wary body language are used efficiently and convincingly throughout. Branagh also hits the right notes in playing the smugly paternalistic bureaucrat so certain the policy of what amounted to legalized kidnapping was in the best interests of the natives, the whites and all of Australia.

Technically, the roving camera, point-of-view photography and mournful sound and music effects all add to the haunting quality of a movie that will resonate long after its unforgettable final scene: footage of the now elderly Molly and Gracie, and an on-screen scroll of what became of Daisy and the sisters. It's fodder for another movie, and in fact Noyce is interested in picking up the story several years later using the same actors. Now that would be a sequel worth seeing.

An inspirational story beautifully filmed, "Rabbit-Proof Fence" deserves to be submitted for foreign-film Oscar consideration by Australia.

Because of some menacing scenes and a theme of racial bias against indigenous peoples, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
